--- execute: eval: true df-print: paged --- # Data objects ::: {.cell} ::: Everything you store in R is an **object**: a single number, a table, or the result of a statistical test. Everything you do with these objects is a **function call**. Objects differ in two ways: - the **data type**: what kind of values they hold, for example numbers or text - the **data structure**: how these values are organised, for example as a single row of values (a vector) or as a table (a data frame) Many functions only work on certain types and structures. A mean of text makes no sense, for example. So when something does not work, the first thing to check is what kind of object you have. ## Data types These are the data types you will use most: | Type | Example | What it holds | |------------------------|------------------------|------------------------| | character | `"hello"`, `"low_P"` | text, always written in quotes | | numeric | `3`, `14.5` | numbers | | logical | `TRUE`, `FALSE` | yes/no values, for example the result of a comparison | Numbers come in two variants: **double** (any number, with or without decimals) and **integer** (whole numbers, written with an `L`, like `2L`). R uses doubles unless you ask for integers, and for most work you do not need to care about the difference. Both count as numeric. R knows two more data types, complex (`1+4i`) and raw, but you will rarely meet them in biology. Two functions help you find out what you have: - `class()` tells you what kind of object you have - `length()` tells you how many values it holds ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #create some objects character_object <- "dataset" number_object <- c(1,4,5) #asking with what type we work class(character_object) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "character" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} class(number_object) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "numeric" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #ask how long our objects are length(character_object) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} length(number_object) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3 ``` ::: ::: ## Data structures The data structures you will meet most often are: - vectors - factors - matrices - lists - data frames You do not have to tell R in advance what an object will hold. When you assign something with `<-`, R picks the data type and structure for you. ### Vectors A vector is a row of values of the same type, for example only numbers or only text. If you mix numbers and text in one vector, R turns the numbers into text. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #lets create a random vector a_vector <- c(2, 3, 5, 7, 1) #show the vector we just created a_vector ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 3 5 7 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #asking how long your vector is length(a_vector) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5 ``` ::: ::: #### Vector indexing If we want to only retrieve part of the data stored in a vector we can create a subset using the index as shown below. - square brackets \[\] = allow us to retrieve certain elements of a vector, i.e. \[3\] retrieves the 3rd element - we can combine `c()` and \[\] if we want to retrieve several elements of a vector. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #retrieve the third element stored in a vector a_vector[3] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #retrieve the 1st and 3rd element by combining ``c()`` and [] a_vector[c(1,3)] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 5 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #retrieve the 1-3rd element a_vector[c(1:3)] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 3 5 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #we can also add vectors of the same length together x <- c(1,2,3,4) y <- c(1,2,3,4) #and now we can combine our vectors x + y ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 4 6 8 ``` ::: ::: Be careful when you add two vectors of different lengths. R then repeats the shorter vector until it is as long as the longer one. This is called **recycling**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #adding vectors of different lengths x <- c(1,2) y <- c(1,2,3,4) #x is repeated: 1+1, 2+2, 1+3, 2+4 x + y ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 4 4 6 ``` ::: ::: If the length of the longer vector is not a multiple of the shorter one, R still recycles, but gives a warning. A warning is not an error: you still get a result, so read warnings carefully. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #x is repeated, but does not fit: 1+1, 2+2, 1+3 x <- c(1,2) y <- c(1,2,3) x + y ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning in x + y: longer object length is not a multiple of shorter object length ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 4 4 ``` ::: ::: Another way to extend vectors is: - `append()` --\> Add elements to a vector. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #add another datapoint to our vector a_vector <- append(a_vector, 13) a_vector ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 3 5 7 1 13 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #add +1 to all our four numbers a_vector <- a_vector + 1 a_vector ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3 4 6 8 2 14 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #remove the first element of our vector a_vector <- a_vector[-1] a_vector ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4 6 8 2 14 ``` ::: ::: We can also give the elements of a vector names, and then use the names to get data: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #create a vector and give it names (i.e. for counts from some microbes) x <- c(300, 410, 531) names(x) <- c("Ecoli","Archaeoglobus","Ignicoccus") #check how our data looks x ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Ecoli Archaeoglobus Ignicoccus 300 410 531 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #now we can retrieve part of the vector using the names x[c("Ecoli","Ignicoccus")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Ecoli Ignicoccus 300 531 ``` ::: ::: #### Changing vectors We can also change elements in our vector: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #create a vector x <- 1:10 #change the second last positions to 5 and 9 x[9:10] <- c(5,9) #check if this worked x ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 5 9 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #we can not only add things, we can also remove this using the minus symbol #i.e. lets remove the third element in our vector x[-3] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 2 4 5 6 7 8 5 9 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} #if we want to remove more than one thing we can use the **c()** #lets remove elements 4 until (and including) 9 x[-c(4:9)] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 2 3 9 ``` ::: ::: #### Useful functions for vectors Apart from the basic math operators, R has many functions that work on vectors. Some common ones are `log()`, `exp()`, `sqrt()` and the following: | Name | Function | |------------|---------------------------------------| | `max()` | select the largest element | | `min()` | select the smallest element | | `length()` | give the number of elements | | `sum()` | sum all elements | | `mean()` | calculate the mean value | | `var()` | calculate the sample variance | | `sort()` | sort the elements from small to large | ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #create a vector x <- c(4, 8, 1, 5) #try some of the functions max(x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 8 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mean(x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4.5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sort(x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 4 5 8 ``` ::: ::: ### Matrices A matrix is a table in which all values have the same type, usually numbers. You will not build many matrices yourself, but you will meet them in other people's code and as the output of some functions, for example tables of counts or distances. Many functions that work on data frames also work on matrices, such as `[rows, columns]`, `dim()` and `head()`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #make a matrix with the numbers 1 to 12 in 4 rows, filled row by row matrix_A <- matrix(1:12, nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE) #check how our matrix looks matrix_A ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [1,] 1 2 3 [2,] 4 5 6 [3,] 7 8 9 [4,] 10 11 12 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #the value in the 2nd row and 3rd column matrix_A[2,3] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 6 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} #the number of rows and columns dim(matrix_A) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4 3 ``` ::: ::: ### Lists A list is a collection of objects that can each have a different type and length: a few numbers, some text, a whole table, or even another list. You create a list with `list()`. For example, here we store cell counts (numeric), the names of the microbes (character) and whether they are alive (logical) in one list: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #define our vectors n = c(20, 30, 50) s = c("Ecoli", "Archaeoglobus", "Bacillus") b = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE) #combine the vectors in a list our_list = list(counts=n, strain=s, status=b) #show our list our_list ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $counts [1] 20 30 50 $strain [1] "Ecoli" "Archaeoglobus" "Bacillus" $status [1] TRUE FALSE TRUE ``` ::: ::: You get one element out of a list with `$` and its name, the same way you get one column out of a data frame: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #get the element with the name strain our_list$strain ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Ecoli" "Archaeoglobus" "Bacillus" ``` ::: ::: Why should you care about lists? Because the results of many functions are lists. For example, a t-test (which we use in the statistics chapter) gives you a list with the test statistic, the p-value and more. With `names()` you see what is inside, and with `$` you take out the part you need: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #compare the root length between the two phosphate levels result <- t.test(Rootlength ~ Nutrient, data = growth_data) #what kind of object is this, and what is inside? class(result) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "htest" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} names(result) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "statistic" "parameter" "p.value" "conf.int" "estimate" [6] "null.value" "stderr" "alternative" "method" "data.name" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} #take out only the p-value result$p.value ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 7.324612e-68 ``` ::: ::: ### Dataframes You already know data frames from the chapter "First steps in R": our growth data is one. A data frame is a table in which each column is a vector. All columns have the same length, and each column has one data type, but different columns can have different types. In our growth data, `Nutrient` is text and `Rootlength` is numeric. So a data frame is a bit like a list of vectors of equal length. Everything you learned about `[rows, columns]` and `$` in "First steps in R" works on data frames. A few more functions are useful to look at them: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #the column names colnames(growth_data) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Nutrient" "Condition" "Experiment" "Rootlength" "FW_shoot_mg" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} #the first few row names head(rownames(growth_data)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "1" "2" "3" "4" "5" "6" ``` ::: ::: When you read a table into R, the rows get the numbers 1 to 594 as row names, unless you say otherwise. You add a new column with `$` and a new column name. Here we fill all rows with the word `comment`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #add a new column growth_data$newColumn <- "comment" #check if that worked head(growth_data) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: You will see this way of adding columns often in other people's code. In the next chapter you learn another way, `mutate()`. ## Check the structure of our data When you read in your own data, check how R stored it: - `class()` tells you what kind of object you have - `str()` (short for structure) shows the data type of each column and the first few values ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #check what kind of data we have: class(growth_data) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "data.frame" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #check how are different parts of our data stored? str(growth_data) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 'data.frame': 594 obs. of 6 variables: $ Nutrient : chr "low_P" "low_P" "low_P" "low_P" ... $ Condition : chr "mock" "mock" "mock" "mock" ... $ Experiment : chr "ex61" "ex61" "ex61" "ex61" ... $ Rootlength : num 40.4 38 74.7 34.4 31.9 66.5 34.8 43.4 33.9 41.9 ... $ FW_shoot_mg: num 6.6 6.8 8.1 8.3 8.6 8.9 9.5 9.8 10 10.2 ... $ newColumn : chr "comment" "comment" "comment" "comment" ... ``` ::: ::: We see that - our data is stored in a data frame - the columns have different data types: `chr` (character) and `num` (numeric) - our data contains 594 observations (rows) and 6 variables (columns): the 5 columns of our file plus the column `newColumn` we added above ## Factors A factor is a vector for **categorical data**: data that falls into a fixed set of groups, such as our nutrient levels or treatments. The possible groups are called **levels**. Factors matter for statistics and for plotting, for example because the order of the levels sets the order of the groups in a plot. By default, R sorts the levels alphabetically. You make a factor with `factor()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #lets make a vector Nutrients <- c("low_P", "low_P", "high_P", "high_P") #lets make our own simple factor Nutrients_factor <- factor(Nutrients) #lets compare the vector and factor we generated Nutrients ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "low_P" "low_P" "high_P" "high_P" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} Nutrients_factor ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] low_P low_P high_P high_P Levels: high_P low_P ``` ::: ::: When we check our factor, we see that R assigns one level to `low_P` and another level to `high_P`. We can also see that R sorts the levels in alphabetical order, i.e. first we have `high_P` and then `low_P`, even though in our vector `low_P` came first. ### Checking the behaviour of factors Now, lets check how factors behave. - `levels()` shows the levels of a factor - `nlevels()` shows how many levels there are - Factors look like text, but R stores them as whole numbers (integers), one number per level. `class()` shows that we have a factor, `typeof()` shows how R stores it: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #only print the levels levels(Nutrients_factor) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "high_P" "low_P" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #check how many levels we have nlevels(Nutrients_factor) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #what class do we have class(Nutrients_factor) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "factor" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} typeof(Nutrients_factor) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "integer" ``` ::: ::: ### Ordering factor levels Often the alphabetical order is not the order you want. In a plot, you may want `low_P` before `high_P`, or the control first. With the argument `levels` you set the order yourself: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #check our levels levels(Nutrients_factor) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "high_P" "low_P" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #reorder levels Nutrients_factor_reordered <- factor(Nutrients_factor, levels = c("low_P", "high_P")) #check our levels levels(Nutrients_factor_reordered) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "low_P" "high_P" ``` ::: ::: ### Converting factors Sometimes you need to turn a factor back into text. You do this with `as.character()`. There are similar functions for other types, such as `as.numeric()`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #convert our factor to a character Nutrients_characters <- as.character(Nutrients_factor) Nutrients_characters ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "low_P" "low_P" "high_P" "high_P" ``` ::: :::
